The Committee’s rate cut to 1.50–1.75% in the face of below-target inflation, weak business fixed investment, and soft exports is consistent with modern monetary policy guidance from New Keynesian frameworks (Galí and Gertler 1999; Woodford 2003), which recommend easing when expected inflation is below target and downside risks to the output gap rise. Given low market-based inflation compensation and largely stable survey-based expectations, the literature suggests limited risk of an inflation overshoot while policy supports demand. The interest-rate channel should bolster investment and inventories (standard investment–interest rate linkage; Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein 1994 on financing sensitivities), and the Open Market Desk’s bill purchases and repo operations mainly ensure smooth policy transmission via ample reserves, aligning with liquidity-effect mechanics rather than signaling a higher inflation objective. In an open-economy context (Obstfeld–Rogoff; surveys by Lane and Engel), global headwinds justify pre-emptive easing. While dissents underscore uncertainty, the literature overall supports a cautiously positive outlook: continued expansion with muted inflation pressures and appropriate policy accommodation.
